maml:description.maml:para: Reads a text file, detecting its character encoding.
Reads a text file and writes its content to the pipeline as strings, one object per line.
When -Encoding is omitted the character encoding of the file is detected. A byte order mark at the start of the file is always skipped, so U+FEFF never leaks into the first line.
Unlike the built-in Get-Content, the same name passed to -Encoding produces the same result on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x.
Path to the target file. Wildcards are permitted.

Character encoding used to decode the file. When omitted (or set to Auto) the file is detected. When specified, no detection is performed, which is the way to override a misdetection. A byte order mark at the start of the file is always skipped, whatever is specified here. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted.

Returns the entire file as a single string instead of splitting it into lines. This is the only lossless way to read a file: splitting into lines discards whether each line ended with CR-LF or LF, and whether the file ended with a line break at all. Cannot be combined with -TotalCount.
Reads only the first N lines of each file. Cannot be combined with -Raw.

Culture name used when detecting the character encoding, such as ko-KR. Combinations that the bytes alone cannot tell apart - EUC-KR and CP949, or EUC-JP and Shift_JIS - are resolved with the culture, so specify the culture of the target language when reading Korean or Chinese files on a Japanese system. Defaults to the culture of the current session. The name and the accepted values are the same as Resolve-Encoding -Culture. Has no effect when the character encoding is given explicitly, because no detection is performed then.

Detection strategy: Combined (default), NativeOnly or UtfUnknownOnly. Combined runs the built-in detector first and falls back to UTF.Unknown only when it cannot decide. The built-in detector covers East Asian multibyte encodings and UTF.Unknown covers Western single-byte encodings, so UtfUnknownOnly is the way to read a Western text that the built-in detector misreads. The name and the accepted values are the same as Resolve-Encoding -Strategy.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.
Detection reads the whole file. A source file whose first megabyte is pure ASCII and which contains Japanese comments only near the end is therefore detected correctly.
Detection failure and a missing file are reported as non-terminating errors, as with the built-in Get-Content. Use -ErrorAction Stop to turn them into terminating errors.
Reading and writing the same file in one pipeline is rejected, because the downstream command would truncate the file before it has been read. Receive the content into a variable first.

maml:description.maml:para: Writes a text file with the character encoding, BOM and line break stated explicitly.
Writes content to a file, replacing anything the file contained.

The same name passed to -Encoding produces the same bytes on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. In particular, 'utf8NoBOM' writes UTF-8 without a BOM on both, which the built-in Set-Content cannot do on PowerShell 5.1.

When -Encoding is omitted, the character encoding, the BOM and the line break are inherited from the file being overwritten, so overwriting does not silently change the nature of an existing file. To inherit from the file the content was read from instead, use -EncodingFrom.
Path to the target file. Wildcards are permitted. The file is created if it does not exist, unless the character encoding has to be inherited from it (see -Encoding).

Content to write. Each element is written followed by a line break, including the last one, unless -NoNewline is specified. Values that are not strings are converted with the PowerShell type converter, which uses the invariant culture.

Character encoding, and BOM policy, used to write the file. When omitted (or set to Auto) they are inherited from the existing file at the destination; if that file does not exist the command reports an error. Cannot be combined with -EncodingFrom. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted.

Inherits the character encoding, the BOM policy and the line break from the given reference file. The value is used exactly as typed; wildcards are not expanded. An explicit -LineBreak still wins over the inherited line break. Cannot be combined with -Encoding.

Does not write a line break between elements or at the end. Required for a lossless round trip of content read with Get-ProbedContent -Raw. When -LineBreak is also specified a warning is issued, because the line break simply goes unused.

Line break to write: Auto, CrLf, Lf or Cr. Auto inherits the line break from the reference information if there is any (-EncodingFrom, -Encoding Auto, or an EncodingInformation passed to -Encoding), and otherwise uses the operating system default. When the reference file has mixed line breaks, CR-LF is inherited if the file contains any CR-LF and LF otherwise; this rule does not depend on the operating system. Only the line break written after each element is decided; line breaks contained in a value (for example "a`nb") are written as they are. To unify the line breaks in a file, use Convert-ProbedContent.

Writes to a file that has the read-only attribute set, by clearing the attribute temporarily; the attribute is restored after writing, even if writing fails. This switch has no effect on anything else.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

Writing cmdlets do not accept the bare name 'utf8' (nor 'utf-8' or the numeric code page 65001), because PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x disagree on whether it means UTF-8 with or without a BOM. Specify 'utf8NoBOM' or 'utf8BOM'. The same applies to the other Unicode families: use 'unicodeNoBOM' / 'unicodeBOM' and so on. The command fails during parameter binding, before the file is opened, so no partially written file is left behind.

How the line break is decided depends on the form of the value passed to -Encoding. An EncodingInformation object (the output of Resolve-Encoding) carries the line break of the file it was detected from, so the line break is inherited as well. A vocabulary name such as 'utf8NoBOM' carries no line break information, so the operating system default is used unless -LineBreak is specified. -EncodingFrom and the default -Encoding Auto always inherit the line break from the file they read.

When a System.Text.Encoding instance is passed directly, its own GetPreamble() decides whether a BOM is written. [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8 and [System.Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(65001) both return BOM-emitting instances, so passing them writes a BOM. Use (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false) for UTF-8 without a BOM, or simply use the vocabulary names, which state the BOM policy explicitly.

UTF-16 and UTF-32 without a BOM ('unicodeNoBOM', 'bigendianunicodeNoBOM', 'utf32NoBOM', 'bigendianutf32NoBOM') are supported so that every state the detector can report can also be written back, but they are NOT recommended: without a BOM there is no reliable way for another program to tell the byte order, or to tell the file apart from a single-byte encoding.

Errors in the combination of parameters (-Encoding together with -EncodingFrom, or a missing -EncodingFrom reference) are terminating errors. Failures that concern one target file (a missing file for -Encoding Auto, detection failure, a read-only file, writing to a file that is being read) are non-terminating errors.

If the destination exists but is empty, there is nothing to detect, so the default encoding of the running .NET runtime (without a BOM) and the operating system default line break are used. That is the ANSI code page on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and UTF-8 on PowerShell 7.x.

dev:remarks.maml:para: Writes UTF-8 without a BOM on both PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x.
Writes Shift_JIS with CR-LF line breaks. PowerShell 5.1 cannot name Shift_JIS with the built-in cmdlets.
Writes b.txt with the character encoding, BOM and line break of a.txt.
Passing an EncodingInformation object inherits the line break as well as the character encoding and BOM.

maml:description.maml:para: Appends to a text file while keeping its character encoding consistent.
Appends content to the end of a file.
When -Encoding is omitted, the character encoding and the line break of the file being appended to are inherited, which is the natural behaviour for appending.

Whether an append is allowed is decided by the bytes that will actually be written, not by the names of the character encodings. If encoding the content with the specified encoding produces exactly the same bytes as encoding it with the encoding the file already uses, the append is allowed, because the file stays consistent. Otherwise the command reports an error. This is why appending ASCII-only text to a UTF-8 file with -Encoding ascii is allowed, while appending Japanese text to the same file with -Encoding shift_jis is not.
Path to the target file. Wildcards are permitted. The file is created if it does not exist, unless the character encoding has to be inherited from it (see -Encoding).

Content to append. Each element is written followed by a line break, including the last one, unless -NoNewline is specified. Values that are not strings are converted with the PowerShell type converter, which uses the invariant culture.

Character encoding used to append to the file. When omitted (or set to Auto) it is inherited from the file being appended to; if that file does not exist the command reports an error. The BOM part of the value is always ignored. Cannot be combined with -EncodingFrom. maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

The BOM part of -Encoding is always ignored by Add-ProbedContent. Writing a BOM into the middle of a file is never correct, so 'utf8BOM' and 'utf8NoBOM' behave identically here. This applies even when the file does not exist yet and is created by this command. No warning is issued, because inheriting from a file that has a BOM (with -EncodingFrom) is a legitimate use.

Writing cmdlets do not accept the bare name 'utf8' (nor 'utf-8' or the numeric code page 65001), because PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x disagree on whether it means UTF-8 with or without a BOM. Specify 'utf8NoBOM' or 'utf8BOM'. The same applies to the other Unicode families: use 'unicodeNoBOM' / 'unicodeBOM' and so on. The command fails during parameter binding, before the file is opened, so no partially written file is left behind.

How the line break is decided depends on the form of the value passed to -Encoding. An EncodingInformation object (the output of Resolve-Encoding) carries the line break of the file it was detected from, so the line break is inherited as well. A vocabulary name such as 'utf8NoBOM' carries no line break information, so the operating system default is used unless -LineBreak is specified. -EncodingFrom and the default -Encoding Auto always inherit the line break from the file they read.

When a System.Text.Encoding instance is passed directly, its own GetPreamble() decides whether a BOM is written. [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8 and [System.Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(65001) both return BOM-emitting instances, so passing them writes a BOM. Use (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false) for UTF-8 without a BOM, or simply use the vocabulary names, which state the BOM policy explicitly.

UTF-16 and UTF-32 without a BOM ('unicodeNoBOM', 'bigendianunicodeNoBOM', 'utf32NoBOM', 'bigendianutf32NoBOM') are supported so that every state the detector can report can also be written back, but they are NOT recommended: without a BOM there is no reliable way for another program to tell the byte order, or to tell the file apart from a single-byte encoding.
The consistency check cannot be bypassed with -Force. -Force means 'write to a read-only file' and nothing else; use -AllowEncodingChange to permit an encoding change.

The check is applied to each element together with the line break that follows it, so a mismatch that only affects the line break is caught as well (LF is one byte in UTF-8 and two bytes in UTF-16LE). If any element of one input record is rejected, none of that record is written.
A difference in line breaks is allowed and produces no warning. Mixed line breaks in a file are harmless, and switching to LF from a given point on can be intentional.
If the file does not end with a line break, the appended content is joined onto the last line, exactly as with the built-in Add-Content.
Stateful character encodings such as ISO-2022-JP are appended safely: the appended block starts with its own escape sequence and returns to ASCII at the end, so it is complete on its own.

maml:alert.maml:para: All failures of this cmdlet are terminating errors, as with the built-in Out-File: there is always exactly one output file, and a non-terminating error would be repeated for every record arriving from upstream. Set-ProbedContent reports some of the same events (such as a read-only file) as non-terminating errors because it can write to several files.

The formatting layer depends on the host. Between PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x the following can differ: trailing spaces in table rows, the number of blank lines around tables and lists, the truncation mark (three periods or a single ellipsis character), how the width of full-width characters is counted, and the default width when -Width is omitted. Strings are written identically on both hosts.

Omitting -Encoding and specifying Auto mean different things. Omitted: utf8NoBOM for a new or overwritten file, and inherited from the target for -Append. Auto: inherited from the existing output file, which must exist. This differs from Set-ProbedContent, where omitting -Encoding means Auto.

-LineBreak decides only the line break written after each line. Line breaks contained in a string (for example "a`r`nb") are written as they are, as with the built-in Out-File and Set-Content. To unify the line breaks in a file, use Convert-ProbedContent.

Differences from the built-in Out-File: the default character encoding is utf8NoBOM on both PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x (inherited from the target with -Append); -Append checks that the character encoding of the file stays consistent; the file is created or truncated just before the first line is written rather than when the command starts; passing a single $null creates an empty (0-byte) file, whereas Out-File writes only a BOM; the aliases -Path and -LP are available on PowerShell 5.1; and -LiteralPath does not take input from the pipeline.

A BOM is written only when at least one line is written. When no input arrives, the output file is created empty (or truncated to 0 bytes) without a BOM; with -Append an existing file is left untouched.

maml:description.maml:para: Converts the character encoding, BOM and line breaks of existing text files.

Rewrites text files with a different character encoding, BOM or line break. The characters themselves are never changed. Files are selected with -Path or -LiteralPath, or by piping the output of Get-ChildItem; this cmdlet has no -Recurse or filtering of its own.

No character is ever lost. A file that contains bytes that are invalid in the source character encoding, or characters that cannot be represented in the destination character encoding, is not converted and is left as it is; the error message shows the position. There is no option to replace such characters.

Each file is written to a temporary file in the same folder, which then replaces the original, so the original is not damaged if the conversion fails midway. If the result is byte-for-byte identical to the original, the file is not rewritten and its timestamp does not change.
Files to convert. Wildcards are permitted. A path that matches no file is reported as a non-terminating error. Directories are skipped.

Character encoding (and BOM) to convert to. When omitted, the character encoding of the source file is kept. Accepts the unified vocabulary, WebNames, numeric code pages, System.Text.Encoding instances and EncodingInformation objects; Auto is not accepted. Together with -Bom, a bare Unicode name or WebName (utf8, utf-8, unicode, ...) is treated as the name of the family and the BOM is decided by -Bom; without -Bom the rules of the other writing cmdlets apply, so the bare utf8 is rejected. See NOTES for the combinations with -Bom.

Converts to the character encoding, BOM and line break of the given reference file. The value is used exactly as typed. -Bom and -LineBreak override the inherited BOM and line break. Cannot be combined with -Encoding.

Add adds a BOM and Remove removes it. When omitted, the BOM is not changed, unless the name given to -Encoding decides it. Only the five Unicode families can have a BOM: Add for another character encoding is an error, while Remove does nothing.

Line break to convert to: CrLf, Lf or Cr. Every line break in the file (CR-LF, LF and CR) is replaced, and whether the last line ends with a line break is kept. U+2028, U+2029 and U+0085 are not treated as line breaks. Auto, the default, keeps the line breaks, or inherits them from -EncodingFrom or an EncodingInformation. Unlike -LineBreak of the writing cmdlets, this unifies all line breaks in the file.

Character encoding of the source files. When omitted (or Auto), it is detected for each file. Specify it to avoid a misdetection; the same values as Get-ProbedContent -Encoding are accepted, including the bare utf8. A BOM at the start of the file is skipped when it matches this character encoding.

Culture name used when detecting the character encoding of the source files, such as ko-KR. Not used when -SourceEncoding is given. The name and the accepted values are the same as Resolve-Encoding -Culture.

Detection strategy used for the source files: Combined (default), NativeOnly or UtfUnknownOnly. Not used when -SourceEncoding is given. The name and the accepted values are the same as Resolve-Encoding -Strategy.

Folder to write the converted files to, keeping their file names. When omitted, the files are converted in place. The folder must exist; it is not created. The folder structure of the sources is not kept: all files are written directly under this folder. With -Destination a file is written even if the result is identical to the source.

Converts read-only files by clearing the attribute temporarily; the attribute is restored afterwards. With -Destination, an existing file of the same name is overwritten. A file already written by the same command is never overwritten.

Outputs one object per converted file, including files that did not need to change, with the properties Path, Destination, SourceEncoding, Encoding, SourceLineBreak, LineBreak and Changed. By default the cmdlet outputs nothing.

Shows what would happen if the cmdlet runs. No file is modified, and nothing is output with -PassThru.
You can pipe objects that have a PSPath property, such as the output of Get-ChildItem.

With -PassThru, one object per converted file, whose type name is SnowStack.EncodingProbe.ConvertResult. Character encodings are named in the unified vocabulary (utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, shift_jis, ...), so passing SourceEncoding back to -Encoding restores the original bytes.

maml:alert.maml:para: A file that contains bytes that are invalid in the source character encoding, or characters that cannot be represented in the destination character encoding, is not converted. The error shows the byte offset of the first invalid bytes, or the first unrepresentable character with its line and column. There is no way to convert such a file by replacing the characters; edit the text first if replacing them is acceptable.

-LineBreak of this cmdlet replaces every line break in the file. -LineBreak of Set-ProbedContent, Add-ProbedContent and Out-ProbedFile only decides the line break written after each element and leaves line breaks inside the strings as they are.

-Encoding and -Bom: a name with a BOM suffix (utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, ...) must agree with -Bom; a bare Unicode name or WebName (utf8, utf-8, unicode, ...) takes its BOM from -Bom; for other character encodings (shift_jis, 932, ...) -Bom Add is an error and -Bom Remove is allowed; the BOM of an EncodingInformation or of -EncodingFrom can be overridden by -Bom; a System.Text.Encoding instance must agree with -Bom. When -Encoding is omitted, the source character encoding is kept, and -Bom Add on a source that cannot have a BOM is reported as an error for that file.
Each source file is read into memory as a whole, so a very large file requires a corresponding amount of memory.

-Destination does not keep the folder structure. When two sources have the same file name, the second one is reported as an error even with -Force, so that a file written by the same command is not overwritten.

Characters in the Private Use Area, such as the HKSCS-specific characters of Hong Kong Big5, are converted as code points without a warning. Converting such a Big5 file to UTF-8 and back to Big5 restores the original bytes.

Errors in the parameters (nothing to convert, -Encoding Auto, conflicting BOM requests, a missing -Destination folder, ...) are terminating errors. Failures that concern one file are non-terminating errors; that file is left unchanged and the other files are still processed.

dev:remarks.maml:para: Converts the text files in the current folder to UTF-8 without a BOM and LF line breaks, detecting the character encoding of each file.
Removes the BOM without having to know the character encodings. Files that cannot have a BOM are left as they are.

maml:description.maml:para: Converts a unified vocabulary name, a code page or a detection result to a System.Text.Encoding object.
Resolves the many forms this module accepts for a character encoding into a single System.Text.Encoding instance.

This is a specialised command, meant for calling .NET class library APIs (System.IO.StreamReader, System.IO.File, XmlWriter and so on) directly from PowerShell. If you only want to read or write files, use Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent or Add-ProbedContent instead; they take exactly the same values for -Encoding and you do not have to convert anything yourself.
The value is treated as being for reading, so names whose BOM policy is undefined ('utf8', 'utf-8', 65001) and 'utf7' are accepted. Auto is rejected, because there is no file to detect.

The value to convert. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted. Auto is not accepted.

The value to convert. Unified vocabulary: Auto, utf8NoBOM, utf8BOM, unicodeNoBOM, unicodeBOM, bigendianunicodeNoBOM, bigendianunicodeBOM, utf32NoBOM, utf32BOM, bigendianutf32NoBOM, bigendianutf32BOM, ascii, ansi, oem, utf7 (reading only). Any WebName known to .NET (shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, big5, gb18030, ...), any numeric code page (932, 65001, ...), a System.Text.Encoding instance, and an EncodingInformation object returned by Resolve-Encoding are also accepted. Auto is not accepted.
You can pipe a name, a code page, a System.Text.Encoding instance or an EncodingInformation object (the output of Resolve-Encoding) to this cmdlet.
The resolved encoding instance.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

When a System.Text.Encoding instance is passed directly, its own GetPreamble() decides whether a BOM is written. [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8 and [System.Text.Encoding]::GetEncoding(65001) both return BOM-emitting instances, so passing them writes a BOM. Use (New-Object System.Text.UTF8Encoding $false) for UTF-8 without a BOM, or simply use the vocabulary names, which state the BOM policy explicitly.

UTF-16 and UTF-32 without a BOM ('unicodeNoBOM', 'bigendianunicodeNoBOM', 'utf32NoBOM', 'bigendianutf32NoBOM') are supported so that every state the detector can report can also be written back, but they are NOT recommended: without a BOM there is no reliable way for another program to tell the byte order, or to tell the file apart from a single-byte encoding.

The BOM policy of the returned instance follows the name: 'utf8BOM' returns an instance that emits a BOM and 'utf8NoBOM' one that does not. For a bare 'utf8' the instance does not emit a BOM, which is why the writing cmdlets refuse that name instead of guessing.

UTF-7 is obsolete and .NET 5 and later refuse to create it through Encoding.GetEncoding. This cmdlet constructs it directly, so 'utf7' works on both PowerShell 5.1 and 7.x. It is supported for reading legacy data only.

dev:remarks.maml:para: Returns a UTF8Encoding instance that does not emit a BOM.

maml:description.maml:para: Detects the character encoding of a text file.

Detects the character encoding of a file and returns an EncodingInformation object describing it: the code page, the WebName, whether the file has a byte order mark, the line break in use, and the culture the detector assumed.
The object can be passed straight to -Encoding of Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent and Add-ProbedContent, and to ConvertTo-DotNetEncoding.
Path to the file to detect.
Culture name used to resolve ambiguities that the bytes alone cannot settle, such as EUC-JP versus Shift_JIS. Defaults to the culture of the current session.
Detection strategy: Combined (default), NativeOnly or UtfUnknownOnly. Combined runs the built-in detector first and falls back to UTF.Unknown only when it cannot decide.
Returns the license text of this module and of the libraries it uses.
Returns the version of this module.

maml:alert.maml:para: The character encoding names accepted by this module (the unified vocabulary) are the same on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.x. They are NOT the same as the names accepted by the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets on PowerShell 5.1, and they do not necessarily match the PSEncodingName property returned by Resolve-Encoding. Do not pass a name from one system to the other and expect the same result.

The PSEncodingName property means different things on the two hosts: on PowerShell 7.x it is a registered friendly name such as 'utf8BOM', while on Windows PowerShell 5.1 it is only filled in when the result happens to match one of the fixed -Encoding values of 5.1, and is otherwise null. UsePSName says whether the value can be passed to the -Encoding parameter of the built-in cmdlets. The unified vocabulary of Get-ProbedContent, Set-ProbedContent and Add-ProbedContent does not have this problem.
